body: Modern French plates are long and white, with blue strips on both sides. Older, rare plates may have a yellow rear plate and lack the right blue strip.
The French language uses many diacritics, including on the letters é, à, è, ù, â, ê, ô, and ç. The suffix -ux is also a unique clue for French.
The French word for street is 'rue'.
The most common French bollard is a round white post with a pointed top and a grey or red reflector band. A rare variation has a fully red top.
A less common but unique French bollard is round and white with two reflective indented bands, and can also be found in green or yellow.
Rare wedge-shaped bollards with wide rectangular white reflectors on the front and back are also unique to France.
Concrete poles with step-like indents, known as 'ladder' or 'waffle' poles, are common in France and Spain.
Wooden poles and thin octagonal metal poles are very common in rural France.
Small blue rectangular plates, often called 'stickers', are a unique feature found on most wooden and metal utility poles in France.
Diamond-shaped poletops with three wires, known as 'French poletops', are common in France, especially on ladder poles. They are also found in Spain.
Some French poletops have insulators on top, creating a unique arrowhead shape.
France has Generation 4 'smallcam' coverage, which is mounted lower and has a large, sometimes transparent, circular blur. This is common across Western Europe.
Small yellow signs displaying the road number, usually starting with a 'D', are unique to France.
French directional signs are typically white with a black outline that gets thicker at the arrow's point. Smaller places are often written in an italic font.
Town entrance signs in France have a red border with a thin white outline.
French road signs have a red border with a thin white outline, distinguishing them from Spanish signs where the red border reaches the edge.
France, along with Portugal, Spain, and Andorra, often uses flat rectangular signposts. These posts and sign backs can sometimes have unusual, region-specific colors.
Traffic signs with particularly short signposts are very common in France.
France uses chevrons with white arrows on a blue background, which can have one to five arrows. Spain uses the same colors but only with two or four arrows.
French pedestrian signs have five stripes and show a person with a disconnected head. A less common version uses two dashed lines instead of stripes.
French kilometre markers are typically a white rectangle with a yellow or red semicircle on top. Major highways may use square markers with a red top.
Typical French roads have long, spaced-out dashes on the outside.
Middle road lines made of two offset blocks per dash are unique to France.
Middle lines with unusually long dashes can be a good clue for France, though they are also found in the UK.
Road arrows signaling the end of a passing zone are found in France, often where middle dashes are very close together. This arrow style also appears in Spain, Portugal, and Romania.
France uses A-type guardrails, usually without reflectors, distinguishing it from countries like Spain that use yellow reflectors.
Tall rectangular markers on sticks with the colors of the Austrian flag (red-white-red) are a unique feature found on French roads.
French architecture often features stone houses, either unpainted or in pastel colors, with gabled roofs of orange tile or black slate. However, architectural styles vary significantly by region.
House numbers in France are commonly on blue signs with a white serif font, which helps distinguish it from Italy.
The French car brands Peugeot, Renault, and Citroën are extremely common in France.
France is divided into 13 regions and 96 departments. Departments are the primary administrative divisions seen on Google Maps and their logos can appear on infrastructure.
French landline phone numbers begin with 01-05. 01 is Paris, while 02-05 follow a clockwise pattern around the country starting from the northwest.
Each French department has a two-digit number, ordered alphabetically. These numbers appear as the first two digits of 5-digit postal codes and on licence plates.
Most French departments have a unique logo which can appear on infrastructure like bus stops, kilometre markers, and signs. These logos can be very helpful for region-guessing.
The Occitanie region has a red and yellow logo featuring an Occitan cross and vertical stripes.
The Pyrénées-Orientales department uses a flag with red and yellow horizontal stripes (the Senyera). This is similar to the flag of Provence, which has vertical stripes.
Roads with a noticeable red, purple, or burgundy tint are most common in the historical region of Burgundy, between Paris and Dijon.
Dark green road signposts and sign backs are most common in Brittany, around Paris, and in some southern regions.
In the Eure-et-Loir department, sign backs may have a green sticker logo, usually on a dark green back.
In Pas-de-Calais, signposts are dark green and sign backs have a lighter green color, sometimes with the department's green and blue triangle logo.
Road signs with both the post and back painted brown are most common in Seine-et-Marne.
Street signs in the Paris metropolitan area often display the city name, which is unusual for France.
Cuboid stone barriers made of stones and mortar are commonly found on Corsica.
France's tallest mountains are in the southeast (Alps) and on the Spanish border (Pyrenees). The north and west are generally flat, while the south is hillier.
Rural roads surrounded by hedges, reminiscent of the British Isles, are primarily found in the northwest, particularly in Normandy.
Stone pines are commonly found along the southern coast, often planted alongside urban roads.
Forests of Maritime pines are found in the flat landscape of the southwest (Gironde and Landes departments).
Major wine regions in France include the area around Bordeaux, the southern coast, and Champagne, east of Paris.
Sunflowers are mostly found in the southwest of the country, particularly around Toulouse.
Wind turbines are considerably more common in the north of the country.
Black shingle roofs are primarily found in the northwest, with the Loire river as a rough cutoff.
Architecture in Brittany often features black roofs, edge chimneys, black slate walls, and stones surrounding doors and windows.
Roofs in the south of the country are often made of rounded, overlapping tiles of varying colors.
Rows of dark red brick houses, similar to Belgian architecture, are found near the Belgian border.
In and around Toulouse, you will commonly find bright orange brick buildings, often with Mediterranean features like wooden shutters.
Walls made of uneven cream-to-orange stones with mortar and red brick details can be found in towns surrounding Paris.
The French Riviera features architecture similar to Monaco, with palm trees and light-colored buildings with wide balconies.
White houses with colorful timber framing are a staple of Basque architecture.
Alpine architecture, with a light-colored base and extensive wooden elements, is found in the Alps.
Elements of Germanic architecture, like timber framing and half-hip roofs, are concentrated in Alsace.
France has several minority languages, including Alsatian, Basque, Breton, Catalan, Corsican, and Occitan.
The Breton language, found on the Breton peninsula, is a Celtic language that uses the letters k, w, and ñ. The Breton word for street is 'straed'.
Towns with the 'Plou-' prefix are concentrated in Northwestern Brittany.
Alsatian, a dialect of German, is occasionally found in Alsace, often on bilingual street signs.
The Occitan language is found sparsely in the South of France, most often on street signs in big cities. The word for street is similar to the Catalan 'carrer'.
Bilingual signs in Basque are found in the western half of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department. The language uses the letters K, X, and Z, and the word for street is 'karrika'.
On the island of Corsica, you may find bilingual signs in Corsican, a language with many similarities to Italian.
The department of Pyrénées-Orientales, also known as Northern Catalonia, uses the Catalan language on its signage.
Knowing common place name suffixes in France is crucial for region-guessing.
Many French cities are named after the river they are on, often in the format -sur-[river].
Réunion is an overseas department of France east of Madagascar, and counts as France for country streaks.
Saint-Pierre and Miquelon is an overseas collectivity of France south of Newfoundland, Canada, and counts as France for country streaks.
Martinique is an overseas department of France in the Caribbean, and counts as France for country streaks.
Mansard roofs, with steep black shingles and dormer windows, are a common feature of Parisian architecture.
On the island of Belle-Île-en-Mer, you can find typical Brittany houses with colorful façades, covered only by oversaturated Generation 2 imagery.
Lavender fields can be found in the southeast.
Salt farms, which appear as flooded trenches, are unique to the west coastal islands of Île de Ré and Île d'Oléron.
Paris, Lyon, and Marseille are the only French cities divided into municipal arrondissements, which are often indicated on street signs.
Paris uses an iconic green and Prussian blue street sign design with a top arch.
Lyon's street signs have four corner bolts and an uninterrupted white border that cuts a notch for the arrondissement and each bolt.
Marseille's street signs usually feature the city's emblem, a variation of the Greek cross, and have an interrupted white border at the top.
Small signs with "Arrondissement" are found in Bordeaux, even though it's not divided into arrondissements.
Montpellier street signs typically have a blue 'M' in the top left corner.
Street signs with a red slanted fleur-de-lis are unique to Lille.
In the outskirts of Bordeaux, traffic signposts can be a Bordeaux red color.
On the French Riviera, you can find traffic signposts painted azure blue, with a lighter powder blue in Cagnes-sur-mer.
Thin B-type guardrails, typical for Czechia and Slovakia, can be found on highways in the northern half of France.
Rare flags attached to the antenna in Generation 3 coverage can provide excellent region-guessing clues within France.
